title: Midnight in the jail (Acts 16:25–34)
hookLine: Paul and Silas sing hymns in chains, and the jailer asks what must I do

cards: Still in Philippi, a few days later. A slave girl who tells fortunes earns her owners a lot of money. Paul, worn out by her following them around, casts the spirit out of her, and her owners watch their profits walk away.

They drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates, and a crowd joins in. The two are stripped, beaten with rods, thrown into the inner prison, their feet fastened in the stocks. Bruised, bleeding, in the dark.
A night like that could be spent in anger, or fear, or silence.

teach.h: AT MIDNIGHT, PRAYING, THEY PRAISED GOD.
teach.b: Here's what they do instead. In the Douay-Rheims: "And at midnight, Paul and Silas praying, praised God."
The Greek says they were singing hymns. And a detail Luke didn't have to include: "they that were in prison, heard them." Suddenly there's an earthquake.
The foundations shake, every door flies open, and everyone's chains come loose.
The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, since a jailer who lost his prisoners could expect to answer for it.

teach.h: DO THYSELF NO HARM, FOR WE ALL ARE HERE.
teach.b: And Paul cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do thyself no harm, for we all are here." Nobody ran.

teach.h: WHAT MUST I DO, THAT I MAY BE SAVED?
teach.b: The jailer calls for a light, rushes in trembling, falls down before them, and asks: "Masters, what must I do, that I may be saved?"
Their answer is short: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your house.
That same night, the man who locked their feet in the stocks washes their wounds. He and his whole household are baptized. He brings them into his house, sets food before them, and rejoices.
Look at the shape of it: songs in the dark, an open door no one walks through, a jailer washing wounds.
Years later, writing to this same church from another prison, Paul tells the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord always.

how: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours through the day and night, singing psalms and hymns, and the Church counts visiting the imprisoned among the works of mercy.

o: songs of praise Paul and Silas sang at midnight
chants the jailer's household sang at baptism
prayers whispered silently by the prisoners

games.q: the night in Philippi — tap the pairs.
p: prayed and praised God at midnight
asked what must I do to be saved
opened every door and loosed every chain

s: the prisoners escaped when the doors opened
Paul cried out, we all are here. nobody ran.
the jailer washed their wounds that same night
then he and his household were baptized, and he fed them at his house.
Luke says the other prisoners were listening
a small detail: two beaten men singing in the dark, and the cell listening.

games.q: you're Paul. an earthquake has opened every door and loosed your chains. the jailer is about to kill himself. what do you do?
o: slip out in the dark while you can.
cry out: do thyself no harm, for we all are here.
games.why: Paul stops him. the man who locked them in asks what he must do to be saved, washes their wounds, and is baptized with his household.

practice: Think of the hardest place in your life right now, a worry, a room, a relationship, and pick a song you know by heart: a hymn if you have one, Amazing Grace, a Marian hymn, anything from Mass, or any song that has carried you before.
Hum a line of it, or just hear it in your head, right there in the hard place; you don't have to feel cheerful, Paul and Silas had bleeding backs. If you pray, the song can be your prayer.
And if the hard place is that you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Hymns. What Paul and Silas sang at midnight in chains, loud enough for the other prisoners to hear, just before the earthquake. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: they were singing hymns. what Paul and Silas did at midnight, the root of our word hymn.
